title: Removable Pins on a Grid
statement:
Pins stand on distinct points of a grid; pin i is at pins[i] = [row, col]. You may pull out a pin only if at least one other pin still standing shares its row or its column.

You choose the order of removals. Return the largest number of pins you can pull out.

examples.why: The first three are linked through row 0 and column 2, so you can pull two of them. The pin at (3, 3) shares nothing with anyone.
No two pins share a row or a column.
A chain. Pull from the far end inward and only the last pin stays. Pulling a middle pin first would cut the chain in two and cost you one removal.

constraints: No two pins share the same point
hints: Draw an edge between two pins that share a row or column. What do the groups of connected pins have in common?
Inside one connected group you can always pull every pin except one: remove pins in the reverse order of a DFS, leaves first.
So the answer is the number of pins minus the number of connected groups. Union-find over rows and columns finds the groups without comparing every pair.

explain.intuition:
Link two pins if they share a row or column. In one connected group, no matter what you do, the very last pin has nobody left to share a line with, so at least one pin per group stays. And one is enough: take any spanning tree of the group and pull pins leaves first. A leaf always still has its parent standing next to it on a line.

So the answer is pins − groups, and the whole problem becomes counting connected components. A neat trick avoids the O(n²) pair check: treat every row and every column as a node, and let each pin union its row with its column. Pins that share a row or column end up in the same set.
steps: Create a union-find. Use key row for rows and col + 10001 for columns so they never collide.
For every pin, union its row node with its column node.
Count distinct roots among the row and column nodes that appear in some pin. That is the number of groups.
pitfalls: Trying to simulate removals greedily. Pulling a pin in the middle of a chain splits it and loses a removal (example 3).
Mixing row 3 and column 3 into the same union-find node. Offset the column keys.
Counting roots over all 20 002 possible nodes instead of only the rows and columns that are used.

solutions.title: DFS over pins sharing a line
solutions.idea: Compare every pair to build adjacency, then count components with DFS.

solutions.title: Union-find over rows and columns
solutions.idea: Each pin joins its row with its column. Groups of pins are the connected sets of lines.

followups: Return an actual order of removals that achieves the maximum.
Pins can also be removed if they share a diagonal. What changes in the union-find?
